extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary students, and critics studying poetic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetic works (especially tragedy and epic): diction, word-formation, metaphor, style, unity of plot, metre, and appropriate use of the marvelous. Emphasizes genre-appropriate choices and moderation in devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Noun
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noun is a composite significant sound, not marking time, of which no part is in itself significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In compound names we do not use the separate parts as if each were in itself significant (example: in 'Theodorus' the element meaning 'gift' is not independently significant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Verb
rubrics_metrics.description: A Verb is a composite significant sound, marking time, in which, as in the noun, no part is in itself significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbs connote time (e.g., 'he walks' = present, 'he has walked' = past). Inflexion belongs to both noun and verb and expresses relations such as case, number, or mode (questions/commands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence/Phrase Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sentence or Phrase is a composite sound, some parts of which are in themselves significant; it may form a unity either by signifying one thing or by consisting of several parts linked together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Cleon walks' has the significant part 'Cleon'. A long work (the Iliad) can be one by linking together parts, whereas a definition is one by the unity of the thing signified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Word-formation (simple, double, multiple)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may be simple (composed of non-significant elements), double/compound (composed of significant+non-significant or both significant elements), or triple/quadruple/multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many magniloquent compounds (e.g., Hermocaico-xanthus) are multiple in form; choice of compound forms affects diction and genre suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of Words (common/proper, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, extended, contracted, altered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is common or proper, strange, metaphorical, ornamental, newly-coined, extended, contracted, or altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions/examples: 'common or proper' = in general use among a people; 'strange' = used in another country; 'metaphor' = application of an alien name by transference (genus↔species, species↔species, or by analogy); 'newly-coined' = invented by the poet (examples provided); 'extended' = vowel lengthened or syllable inserted; 'contracted' = part removed; 'altered' = part unchanged and part re-cast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor: forms and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, from species to genus, from species to species, or by analogy (proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided (e.g., 'stands my ship' = anchor as species of standing). One may qualify a metaphor by adding the term to which the proper word is relative ('the cup is to Dionysus as the shield to Ares' → 'the shield of Dionysus'). Metaphor-making requires an eye for resemblances and is the greatest achievement in diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Newly-coined Words
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one which has never yet been in use, but is invented by the poet himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include inventive coinages for poetic effect (e.g., terms meaning 'sprouters' or 'supplicator'). Such coinages can give distinction but must be used with taste and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension, Contraction, Alteration as stylistic licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is extended when its vowel is exchanged for a longer one or when a syllable is inserted; contracted when part is removed; altered when part is left unchanged and part re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These deviations from normal idiom provide distinction while partial conformity assures perspicuity. Critics are mistaken to ridicule these licences when used properly; they should not be obtrusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of Style: clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A diction of only common/proper words is highly clear but mean (examples: poetry of Cleophon and Sthenelus). Conversely, wholly unusual diction is lofty but can become a riddle or jargon. Therefore an infusion of rare/figurative/ornamental elements is necessary to raise style above the commonplace while retaining clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riddle vs Jargon: risks of excessive devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly composed of metaphors becomes a riddle; a style wholly of rare or strange words becomes a jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essence of a riddle is expressing true facts under impossible combinations (requires metaphors). A jargon (overuse of rare words) renders meaning inaccessible. Moderate mixture is required to avoid both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and Propriety in Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors, rare/strange words, extensions, contractions, and alterations must be used with moderation and propriety; obtrusive use is grotesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how alteration of a single word can make a line beautiful or trivial (Aeschylus vs Euripides examples). Overuse for ludicrous effect is improper; partial conformity to usage retains perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate Lexical Choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic genres call for different word-types: compound names fit dithyrambs, rare words fit heroic (epic) poetry, metaphors suit iambic verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In iambic verse (imitating familiar speech) the most appropriate words are those of conversational idiom: common/proper, metaphorical, ornamental. In heroic/epic metre all varieties (rare words, metaphors, compounds) are especially serviceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action in Narrative (single metre) and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot of narrative (epic) or tragedy ought to be constructed on dramatic principles: a single action whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces the organism-like unity that yields proper pleasure. Avoid making the subject too vast to be embraced in a single view; select a portion that admits beginning and end (Homer's practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Scale and Inclusion of Episodes in Epic vs Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry differs from tragedy in scale: epic can represent many events and simultaneous actions (narrative form allows many parts), while tragedy must confine itself to the action on the stage and actors' part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic's narrative form permits episodes that add mass and dignity; but scale must remain such that beginning and end can be surveyed. Mixing many incidents without unity leads to lack of proper ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter Suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic (epic) metre is the stateliest and most imposing and has proved its fitness by experience; other metres are less fitting for great-scale narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing different metres is absurd; iambic and trochaic tetrameter suit action and dancing respectively. Nature and experience teach the choice of proper measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial Presence: the poet should speak little
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet in his own person should speak as little as possible; it is not this that makes him an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer is exemplary: after few prefatory words he introduces characters who possess characteristic qualities. Other poets who appear throughout their works imitate little and are inferior in imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Wonderful and the Irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful (the irrational) is admitted in Tragedy and has wider scope in Epic because the actor is not seen; the wonderful is pleasing and can be used to enhance narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some absurdities would be ludicrous on stage (e.g., a pursuit shown awkwardly) but acceptable in epic. Poets may employ the wonderful to delight hearers, using the audience's inclination to accept startling additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Use of Implausibility (probability vs impossibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is preferable to make the improbable appear likely ('ἀδύνατα εἰκότα') rather than to make likely things appear impossible; the poet should aim for 'the improbable but believable' rather than the manifestly false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the second (outcome) is true in the narrative, it may be unnecessary to prove the first (cause); the audience will infer it (example: Bath Scene in Odyssey). Avoid material that would be ludicrous if presented plainly on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of Artifice in Diction and Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let excessively brilliant diction obscure characters' moral qualities or thoughts; wordy splendor should not hide the ethical or intellectual elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language must sometimes 'labour' in slow (argoi) parts but should not conceal the ethical or intellectual content; clarity in the telling of problems/solutions requires naming kinds so the audience can see the structure.
